chunks.text: 2.1 Task-Specific Approaches Medical image segmentation is a cornerstone of computer-aided diagnosis, enabling precise anatomical delineation and lesion quantification. Over the past decade, deep learning has driven substantial progress through several evolving architectural paradigms. Initially, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) dominated the field by leveraging strong inductive biases such as local receptive fields and translation equivariance. Representative U-shaped architectures like U-Net [ 37 ] , CE-Net [ 13 ] , and AAU-Net [ 5 ] effectively preserve spatial details through skip connections and multi-scale feature aggregation. Despite these advancements, the inherent locality of convolutional operations fundamentally restricts their ability to model long-range dependencies, often leading to suboptimal performance when segmenting targets with large shape variations or complex lesion structures. To overcome this issue, transformer-based architectures have been increasingly adopted. Models such as Swin-Unet [ 4 ] and MISSFormer [ 19 ] replace convolutional encoders with hierarchical self-attention mechanisms, enabling global context modeling across the entire image. Nevertheless, such pure transformers lack inherent spatial inductive biases, making them prone to over-smoothing fine-grained boundaries and struggling with low-contrast or small-scale medical targets, especially under limited annotations. Thus, hybrid CNN-Transformer architectures have emerged to combine local feature extraction with global semantic modeling. TransUNet [ 6 ] pioneers this direction by feeding CNN-extracted feature maps into a transformer encoder and fusing high-resolution CNN features via skip connections. TransFuse [ 49 ] adopts a parallel dual-branch design, integrating CNN and transformer pathways through a bidirectional fusion module to simultaneously capture local details and global semantics.

Similarly, H2Former [ 15 ] constructs a hierarchical hybrid block that unifies convolution, multi-scale channel attention, and token-wise self-attention within a single stage. While these hybrid designs improve segmentation accuracy, they often rely on complex, manually engineered fusion strategies and remain heavily dependent on task-specific architectural tuning. Furthermore, the quadratic computational complexity of vanilla self-attention has spurred research into efficient attention mechanisms. Recent works like BRAU-Net++ [ 24 ] , MedFormer [ 42 ] , and MSLAU-Net [ 25 ] introduce sparse [ 10 , 50 ] or linear attention [ 22 ] to scale to higher resolutions. Although these methods significantly reduce computational burdens, they still require extensive task-specific architectural redesign and struggle to generalize across diverse imaging modalities without retraining. This motivates a move away from task-specific architectural engineering toward adapting vision foundation models. 2.2 Segment Anything Model Adaptations While adapting SAM for domain-specific tasks has garnered more attention, achieving effective and robust adaptation for medical image segmentation remains a critical challenge. PEFT has emerged as a promising paradigm, freezing the majority of pretrained weights while updating only a minimal, targeted subset. This strategy drastically reduces computational and memory overhead while preserving the rich, domain-agnostic representations learned in the foundation model. Existing PEFT-based adaptations for SAM can be broadly categorized into three representative categories: prompt-based tuning [ 20 , 27 ] , adapter-based tuning [ 9 , 33 ] , and low-rank adaptation [ 18 ] . Prompt-based methods, such as TP-SAM [ 35 ] and BT-SAM [ 28 ] , introduce learnable continuous vectors into the input or embedding space to steer SAM toward downstream tasks.

While highly parameter-efficient and effective at preserving pretrained knowledge, these prompts primarily operate at the input level. Consequently, they offer limited capacity to explicitly model local texture patterns, fine-grained anatomical structures, and ambiguous boundaries that are paramount in medical imaging. Adapter-based strategies insert lightweight bottleneck modules into transformer layers to bridge the domain gap. Early approaches adopted the conventional adapter design [ 17 ] , which, despite its efficiency, lacks domain-specific inductive biases and often struggles to capture intricate local details. To mitigate this, recent works such as Trans-SAM [ 41 ] , NAS-Adapter [ 7 ] , CC-SAM [ 12 ] and SAMUS [ 29 ] have integrated convolutional operations or parallel CNN branches into the adapter architecture, thereby injecting local spatial priors and enhancing boundary perception. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [ 18 ] represents another dominant PEFT paradigm, approximating weight updates via low-rank matrix decomposition. Recent works like SAMed [ 48 ] apply LoRA to the query and value projection layers of SAM’s image encoder, achieving competitive performance with minimal trainable parameters. Despite these advances, two fundamental limitations remain. First, existing methods predominantly integrate local cues through post-hoc convolutional enhancement or cross-branch fusion, rather than explicitly injecting local structural priors into the core self-attention mechanism. As a result, their influence on the ViT’s long-range dependency modeling remains suboptimal. To address this, we propose the convolutional visual prompting (CVP) strategy, which explicitly prepends CNN-derived local priors to the key and value sequences within multi-head self-attention. Second, most lightweight modules prioritize generic low-dimensional feature transformations, lacking explicit mechanisms to enhance high-frequency boundary information.

This deficiency is particularly detrimental for medical images characterized by low contrast, blurred edges, and subtle texture transitions. Meanwhile, recent frequency-domain analyses in foundation models reveal that task-relevant semantics are usually encoded in high-frequency features, while domain-specific biases reside in low-frequency components [ 26 , 39 ] . Inspired by this, we design a boundary-aware adapter (BAA) that explicitly computes and amplifies high-frequency components to improve feature representations along lesion boundaries. 3 Method 3.1 Overall Framework As illustrated in Fig. 2 , our framework preserves the foundational SAM architecture while systematically enhancing its image encoder to better capture local anatomical structures and boundary details critical for medical image analysis. Inspired by the dual-branch encoding paradigm of SAMUS [ 29 ] , we adopt a parallel feature extraction scheme comprising a ViT branch and a complementary CNN branch . Figure 2: Architecture overview of the proposed CVP-BAA framework for efficient SAM adaptation. The framework consists of two core components: the convolutional visual prompting (CVP) module, which explicitly injects local structural priors into the global self-attention layer, and the boundary-aware adapter (BAA), which isolates and amplifies high-frequency boundary cues. By combining these components, CVP-BAA achieves parameter-efficient adaptation of the frozen SAM backbone, yielding highly precise and robust medical image segmentation. Given an input image of resolution H H × \times W W × \times 3, where H H and W W denote the height and width, respectively, both branches process the image in parallel. In the ViT branch , a patch embedding layer projects the input into a sequence of tokens, establishing a feature resolution of H / 8 {H/8} × \times W / 8 {W/8} , which remains consistent across all subsequent transformer blocks.

Meanwhile, the CNN branch employs a lightweight pathway consisting of one SingleConv layer and three successive SingleConv - MaxPooling blocks, followed by four additional SingleConv layers. Each SingleConv block comprises a 3 × \times 3 convolution, layer normalization, and a GELU activation. This design progressively downsamples the feature maps and refines their representations, ultimately aligning their spatial resolution with that of the ViT branch at H / 8 {H/8} × \times W / 8 {W/8} . To address the inherent limitation of vanilla self-attention in capturing fine-grained local details, we integrate two novel modules into specific global attention transformer blocks. First, we introduce convolutional visual prompting (CVP), as shown in Fig. 3 , a mechanism that explicitly extracts local structural priors from the outputs of the final SingleConv - MaxPooling block and the subsequent three SingleConv blocks in the CNN branch. These priors are injected as visual prompts by being prepended to the key and value projections within the multi-head self-attention (MHSA) layers of the 3 -rd, 6 -th, 9 -th, and 12 -th ViT blocks, thereby enriching long-range dependency modeling with structural cues. Second, we propose the boundary-aware adapter (BAA), as depicted in Fig. 4 , a parallel adaptation module inserted alongside the feed-forward network (FFN). The BAA is specifically designed to compute and amplify high-frequency components of the features, significantly enhancing the representation of tissue boundaries and other subtle anatomical structures. Together, CVP and BAA enable the efficient adaptation of SAM, leading to superior segmentation performance. 3.2 Convolutional Visual Prompting The convolutional visual prompting (CVP) component is designed to inject local structural representations into global dependency modeling. As illustrated in Fig. 3 , it comprises two stages: prompt generation and prompt injection. Prompt Generation . As shown in Fig.

3 (a), let 𝑭 c ∈ ℝ N × C \bm{F}_{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C} denote the feature map produced by the corresponding SingleConv (- MaxPooling ) block of the parallel CNN branch, where N = H ​ W N=HW is the spatial sequence length and C C represents the channel dimension. To enhance local structural representations, we first refine 𝑭 c \bm{F}_{c} using a 1 × 1 1\times 1 convolution to obtain 𝑭 ^ c \hat{\bm{F}}_{c} . Subsequently, a spatial attention mechanism is employed to highlight salient lesion regions. Specifically, average pooling and max pooling are performed on 𝑭 ^ c \hat{\bm{F}}_{c} along the channel dimension, formulated as: 𝑭 avg = AvgPool ⁡ ( 𝑭 ^ c ) , 𝑭 max = MaxPool ⁡ ( 𝑭 ^ c ) , \bm{F}_{\mathrm{avg}}=\mathrm{AvgPool}(\hat{\bm{F}}_{c}),\quad\bm{F}_{\mathrm{max}}=\mathrm{MaxPool}(\hat{\bm{F}}_{c}), (1) where 𝑭 avg , 𝑭 max ∈ ℝ N × 1 \bm{F}_{\mathrm{avg}},\bm{F}_{\mathrm{max}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 1} . These two feature maps are then concatenated along the channel dimension and processed through a 3 × \times 3 convolution followed by a Sigmoid activation function to generate a spatial attention map: 𝑨 = σ ⁡ ( Conv 3 × 3 ​ ( [ 𝑭 avg ; 𝑭 max ] ) ) , \bm{A}=\sigma\left(\mathrm{Conv}_{3\times 3}([\bm{F}_{\mathrm{avg}};\bm{F}_{\mathrm{max}}])\right), (2) where 𝑨 ∈ ℝ N × 1 \bm{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 1} encodes the learned importance weights, and [ ⋅ ; ⋅ ] [\cdot;\cdot] denotes channel-wise concatenation. Finally, the refined visual prompt 𝑷 ∈ ℝ N × C \bm{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C} is obtained by adaptively weighting the local features: 𝑷 = 𝑭 ^ c + 𝑭 ^ c ⊗ 𝑨 , \bm{P}=\hat{\bm{F}}_{c}+\hat{\bm{F}}_{c}\otimes\bm{A}, (3) where ⊗ \otimes denotes element-wise multiplication. This design effectively amplifies boundary-sensitive local structures while preserving the original feature semantics, yielding robust prompts for subsequent injection into the global attention mechanism. Prompt Injection . As illustrated in Fig.

1 (b) and Fig 3 (b), unlike SAMUS [ 29 ] , which injects CNN features via cross-branch attention, we explicitly construct refined visual prompts 𝑷 ∈ ℝ N × C \bm{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C} to generate key and value prompts, denoted as 𝑷 k ∈ ℝ N × C \bm{P}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C} and 𝑷 v ∈ ℝ N × C \bm{P}_{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C} . These are directly prepended to the original key ( 𝑲 ∈ ℝ N × C \bm{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C} ) and value ( 𝑽 ∈ ℝ N × C \bm{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C} ) sequences within the self-attention layers. To enable parallel multi-head computation, we first split the input features and prompts into h h attention heads via a linear operation. Let 𝑸 i , 𝑲 i , 𝑽 i ∈ ℝ N × d h \bm{Q}^{i},\bm{K}^{i},\bm{V}^{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{h}} denote the query, key, and value representations for the i i -th head ( i = 1 , … , h i=1,\ldots,h ), where d h = C / h d_{h}=C/h is the dimension of each head. Similarly, the prompts are partitioned into 𝑷 k i , 𝑷 v i ∈ ℝ N × d h \bm{P}^{i}_{k},\bm{P}^{i}_{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{h}} . The projections for the i i -th head are computed as: 𝑸 i = 𝑸 ​ 𝑾 q i , 𝑲 i = 𝑲 ​ 𝑾 k i , 𝑽 i = 𝑽 ​ 𝑾 v i , \bm{Q}^{i}=\bm{Q}{\bm{W}^{i}_{q}},\quad\bm{K}^{i}=\bm{K}{\bm{W}^{i}_{k}},\quad\bm{V}^{i}=\bm{V}{\bm{W}^{i}_{v}}, (4) and the corresponding prompt projections are obtained by: 𝑷 k i = 𝑷 ​ 𝑾 p ​ k i , 𝑷 v i = 𝑷 ​ 𝑾 p ​ v i , \bm{P}^{i}_{k}=\bm{P}{\bm{W}^{i}_{pk}},\quad\bm{P}^{i}_{v}=\bm{P}{\bm{W}^{i}_{pv}}, (5) where 𝑾 q i , 𝑾 k i , 𝑾 v i , 𝑾 p ​ k i , 𝑾 p ​ v i ∈ ℝ C × d h \bm{W}^{i}_{q},\bm{W}^{i}_{k},\bm{W}^{i}_{v},\bm{W}^{i}_{pk},\bm{W}^{i}_{pv}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times d_{h}} are the learnable projection matrices for the i i -th head.

We then concatenate these prompts along the sequence dimension to augment the original sequences: 𝑲 ~ i = [ 𝑲 i ; 𝑷 k i ] , 𝑽 ~ i = [ 𝑽 i ; 𝑷 v i ] , \tilde{\bm{K}}^{i}=[\bm{K}^{i};\bm{P}^{i}_{k}],\quad\tilde{\bm{V}}^{i}=[\bm{V}^{i};\bm{P}^{i}_{v}], (6) where [ ⋅ ; ⋅ ] [\cdot;\cdot] denotes concatenation along the sequence dimension, yielding updated key and value tensors 𝑲 ~ i , 𝑽 ~ i ∈ ℝ 2 ​ N × d h \tilde{\bm{K}}^{i},\tilde{\bm{V}}^{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{2N\times d_{h}} . The attention output for each head is then computed via the standard scaled dot-product mechanism: head i = Attention ⁡ ( 𝑸 i , 𝑲 ~ i , 𝑽 ~ i ) = Softmax ⁡ ( 𝑸 i ​ ( 𝑲 ~ i ) ⊤ d h ) ​ 𝑽 ~ i . \mathrm{head}_{i}=\mathrm{Attention}(\bm{Q}^{i},\tilde{\bm{K}}^{i},\tilde{\bm{V}}^{i})=\mathrm{Softmax}\left(\frac{\bm{Q}^{i}(\tilde{\bm{K}}^{i})^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{h}}}\right)\tilde{\bm{V}}^{i}. (7) The multi-head outputs are concatenated and linearly projected to produce the final representation: GMHSA ⁡ ( 𝑸 , 𝑲 , 𝑽 ) = Concat ⁡ ( head 1 , … , head h ) ​ W O , \operatorname{GMHSA}(\bm{Q},\bm{K},\bm{V})=\operatorname{Concat}(\mathrm{head}_{1},\ldots,\mathrm{head}_{h})W^{O}, (8) where W O ∈ ℝ C × C W^{O}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times C} is the output projection matrix. GMHA ⁡ ( ⋅ , ⋅ , ⋅ ) \operatorname{GMHA}(\cdot,\cdot,\cdot) denotes the global multi-head self-attention function. In our implementation h = 12 h=12 , C = 768 C=768 , and d h = C / h = 64 d_{h}=C/h=64 . The key advantage of this design lies in the explicit injection of prompt tokens into the attention keys and values. By doing so, the fine-grained local textures and boundary cues extracted by the CNN branch actively participate in global context modeling of the vision transformer while preserving the semantic integrity of the queries inherited from the pre-trained backbone. The CVP consists of two sequential stages: (a) prompt generation, which extracts fine-grained local structural priors via a parallel CNN branch, and (b) prompt injection, which explicitly integrates these local representations into the ViT’s self-attention mechanism to guide global dependency modeling. 3.3 Boundary-Aware Adapter As shown in Fig. 4 , the boundary-aware adapter (BAA) is deployed as a parallel branch alongside the original FFN, consisting of two essential modules: boundary enhancement (BE) and a branch scaling factor s s . Boundary Enhancement . Inspired by the Deep Edge Filter [ 26 ] , we design the boundary enhancement (BE) module as an explicit high-pass filter constructed by subtracting low-pass filtered outputs from input features. We implement the low-pass filtering via a 3 × \times 3 average pooling operation. As depicted in Fig. 4 (left), given the input features 𝑿 n ∈ ℝ N × C \bm{X}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C} from layer normalization, we first project them into a low-dimensional bottleneck space via a linear down projection layer followed by a GELU activation: 𝑭 b = GELU ⁡ ( 𝑿 n ​ 𝑾 d ) , \bm{F}_{b}=\mathrm{GELU}(\bm{X}_{n}\bm{W}_{d}), (9) where 𝑭 b ∈ ℝ N × C \bm{F}_{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C} indicates the bottleneck features, 𝑾 d ∈ ℝ C × d r \bm{W}_{d}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times{d_{r}}} denotes the down projection matrix, and d r ≪ C d_{r}\ll C is the bottleneck dimension. Then, we employ a 3 × \times 3 average pooling operation as the low-pass filter on 𝑭 b \bm{F}_{b} to yield the low-pass filtered results 𝑭 l \bm{F}_{l} , and the generalizable, task-specific high-frequency representations 𝑭 h \bm{F}_{h} are isolated by subtracting 𝑭 l \bm{F}_{l} from 𝑭 b \bm{F}_{b} : 𝑭 l = AvgPool 3 × 3 ​ ( 𝑭 b ) , 𝑭 h = 𝑭 b − 𝑭 l . \bm{F}_{l}=\mathrm{AvgPool}_{3\times 3}(\bm{F}_{b}),\quad\bm{F}_{h}=\bm{F}_{b}-\bm{F}_{l}.

(10) Subsequently, the bottleneck feature 𝑭 b \bm{F}_{b} and the extracted boundary component 𝑭 h \bm{F}_{h} are concatenated along the channel dimension and fused through a 1 × \times 1 convolution: 𝑭 f = Conv 1 × 1 ​ ( [ 𝑭 b ; 𝑭 h ] ) . \bm{F}_{f}=\mathrm{Conv}_{1\times 1}\left([\bm{F}_{b};\bm{F}_{h}]\right). (11) Finally, 𝑭 f \bm{F}_{f} is activated by GELU and projected back to the original dimension via an up-projection matrix 𝑾 u ∈ ℝ d r × C \bm{W}_{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{r}\times C} , producing the BE Adapter (denoted as BEA) output: BEA ⁡ ( 𝑿 n ) = GELU ⁡ ( 𝑭 f ) ​ 𝑾 u . \mathrm{BEA}(\bm{X}_{n})=\mathrm{GELU}(\bm{F}_{f})\bm{W}_{u}. (12) Branch Scaling Factor s s . Following prior work on adapter-based fine-tuning [ 8 , 16 , 21 ] and branch scaling [ 47 ] , we introduce a scaling factor s s to balance the contribution of the adapter branch relative to the frozen transformer pathway. The BE Adapter output is integrated into the FFN via element-wise summation: 𝑿 ′ = FFN ⁡ ( 𝑿 n ) + s ⋅ BEA ⁡ ( 𝑿 n ) , \bm{X}^{\prime}=\mathrm{FFN}(\bm{X}_{n})+s\cdot\mathrm{BEA}(\bm{X}_{n}), (13) where FFN ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathrm{FFN}(\cdot) denotes the original feed-forward network and 𝑿 ′ \bm{X}^{\prime} serves as the input to subsequent transformer blocks. As a hyperparameter, s s is helpful for the trade-off between the primary semantic pathway and the high-frequency adapter branch, and thus preventing optimization instability during early training stages. Our ablation studies demonstrate that setting s = 0.3 s=0.3 yields optimal segmentation performance. Figure 4: Architecture of the proposed boundary-aware adapter (BAA). The BAA comprises a boundary enhancement (BE) module and a branch scaling factor s s . The BE module acts as an explicit high-pass filter to compute and amplify the high-frequency components of the feature maps, enhancing the representation of fine-grained structures and boundaries.

Concurrently, the scaling factor s s serves as a crucial regularizer, balancing the contribution of the high-frequency adapter branch against the primary frozen transformer backbone. In all our experiments, λ \lambda is empirically set to 0.8 0.8 .

4 Experimental Settings 4.1 Datasets To comprehensively evaluate the performance and generalization capability of CVP-BAA, we conduct experiments on five publicly available datasets: BUSI [ 1 ] , UDIAT [ 45 ] , TN3K [ 11 ] , CVC-ClinicDB [ 3 ] , and ISIC-2018 [ 34 ] . These datasets span three representative medical imaging modalities: ultrasound, endoscopy, and dermoscopy. Ultrasound imaging is particularly challenging due to inherent artifacts such as low contrast, speckle noise, and ambiguous lesion boundaries, making it a rigorous benchmark for assessing boundary-aware segmentation. Thus, we incorporate two breast ultrasound datasets (BUSI and UDIAT) alongside one thyroid ultrasound dataset (TN3K). Furthermore, to thoroughly assess cross-domain generalization, we include the CVC-ClinicDB dataset for endoscopy and the ISIC-2018 dataset for dermoscopy. This deliberately curated, multi-modality benchmark is designed to rigorously validate the robustness and broad clinical applicability of the proposed adaptation method. 4.1.1 BUSI The BUSI dataset contains 780 breast ultrasound images with pixel-wise annotations, acquired using LOGIQ E9 and LOGIQ E9 Agile scanners. All the images have an average resolution of 500 × \times 500 pixels in PNG format. To ensure fair comparison, we adopt the same data split as SAMUS [ 29 ] , dividing the dataset into training, validation, and testing sets with a 7:1:2 ratio. 4.1.2 UDIAT The UDIAT dataset comprises 163 pixel-wise annotated ultrasound images from female patients, each containing one or more lesions. The images are acquired using a Siemens ACUSON Sequoia C512 system with an 8.5 MHz 17L5 HD linear array transducer and have a mean resolution of 760 × \times 570 pixels. For our experiments, the dataset is partitioned into 115 training, 16 validation, and 32 testing images.

4.1.3 TN3K The TN3K dataset comprises 3,493 thyroid ultrasound images with pixel-wise nodule annotations, collected across three different ultrasound imaging systems: RESONA 70B, ARIETTA 850, and GE Logiq E9. Following the data partitioning protocol established by SAMUS [ 29 ] and TRFE+ [ 11 ] , we divide the dataset into 2,303 training, 576 validation, and 614 testing samples. 4.1.4 CVC-ClinicDB The CVC-ClinicDB dataset consists of 612 colonoscopy images, originally utilized as the benchmark for the MICCAI 2015 Sub-Challenge on Automatic Polyp Detection. In our experiments, the dataset is randomly partitioned into 490 images for training, 61 for validation, and 61 for testing. 4.1.5 ISIC-2018 The ISIC-2018 dataset is widely recognized for benchmarking skin lesion segmentation methods. It comprises 2,594 clinical dermoscopy images with varying resolutions, which are randomly partitioned into 1,868 training images, 467 validation images, and 259 testing images, respectively. 4.2 Evaluation Metrics To ensure a fair comparison with state-of-the-art methods and to comprehensively evaluate the performance of CVP-BAA, we employ six standard segmentation metrics: Dice coefficient (Dice), Hausdorff distance (HD), mean Intersection over Union (mIoU), Accuracy (Acc), Precision (Prec), and Recall (Rec). For the ultrasound datasets: BUSI, UDIAT, and TN3K, we report Dice and HD; for ISIC-2018 and CVC-ClinicDB, we report Dice, mIoU, Acc, Prec, and Rec. Additionally, we assess computational efficiency through the number of parameters (#Params), floating-point operations (FLOPs), and inference speed (FPS). All results are reported as mean ± \pm standard deviation over three independent runs with different random seeds to verify the robustness and generalizability of the proposed CVP-BAA. 4.3 Implementation Details We adopt the pre-trained SAM with a ViT-B backbone, originally trained on the SA-1B dataset, as our foundational architecture.

All three components in this version of SAM, namely, the image encoder, prompt encoder, and mask decoder, remain frozen during training. Only the parameters of the parallel CNN branch, along with the CVP and BAA components, are optimized. All experiments are conducted on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU with 24 GB of memory. The models are trained for 200 epochs using the Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of 1 ​ e − 4 1e-4 and a batch size of 8. The training objective is supervised by a hybrid loss function combining Dice loss and binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss. In addition, following the protocol of SAMUS [ 29 ] , we employ a single-point prompt for interaction, and all input images are uniformly resized to 256 × \times 256 pixels. 4.1 Datasets To comprehensively evaluate the performance and generalization capability of CVP-BAA, we conduct experiments on five publicly available datasets: BUSI [ 1 ] , UDIAT [ 45 ] , TN3K [ 11 ] , CVC-ClinicDB [ 3 ] , and ISIC-2018 [ 34 ] . All results are reported as mean ± \pm standard deviation over three independent runs with different random seeds to verify the robustness and generalizability of the proposed CVP-BAA. 5 Experimental Results 5.1 Comparisons with other methods We evaluate CVP-BAA against a comprehensive suite of state-of-the-art baselines. This includes representative task-specific architectures spanning CNN-based models like UNet [ 37 ] and AAU-Net [ 5 ] , pure transformer frameworks such as Swin-Unet [ 4 ] and MISSFormer [ 19 ] , and hybrid CNN-Transformer models including TransFuse [ 49 ] , H2Former [ 15 ] , and BRAU-Net++ [ 24 ] . Additionally, we benchmark our method against leading SAM adaptation strategies, namely vanilla SAM [ 23 ] , MedSAM [ 31 ] , SAMed [ 48 ] , and Med-SA [ 40 ] . 5.1.1 Comparison on BUSI, UDIAT, and TN3K Quantitative Results . The quantitative results are presented in Table 4 , and the visualizations are illustrated in Fig. 8 . For our ablation study, we employ a modified version of SAMUS [ 29 ] as the baseline. Specifically, this baseline omits the original cross-branch attention (CBA) and standard adapter modules, replacing the CBA mechanism with a simple element-wise summation to fuse CNN-derived features into the ViT encoder. 5.2.1 Effectiveness of CVP The integration of solely the CVP component into the baseline architecture leads to consistent and substantial segmentation gains: +2.12% in Dice and -1.97 mm in HD on the BUSI dataset, and +2.30% in Dice and -1.48 mm in HD on the TN3K dataset, respectively. These results validate that CVP effectively injects local fine-grained details to guide global dependency modeling and provides complementary cues for accurate lesion localization.

5.2.2 Effectiveness of BAA Integrating the BAA component alone into the baseline yields consistent performance improvements: achieving a +3.58% gain in Dice and a -2.83 mm reduction in HD on the BUSI dataset, alongside a +3.09% gain in Dice and a -1.97 mm reduction in HD on the TN3K dataset. This indicates that incorporating the BAA significantly boosts performance, confirming its specific effectiveness in enhancing high-frequency boundary delineation and reducing boundary errors. 5.2.3 Effectiveness of Combinations Combining both CVP and BAA achieves the best performance across both datasets, yielding 86.71% Dice and 24.52 mm HD on BUSI, alongside 85.23% Dice and 27.77 mm HD on TN3K. These results demonstrate that CVP and BAA work in concert, enabling a highly effective adaptation of SAM for medical image segmentation. Fig. 5 presents the qualitative segmentation results across the BUSI, UDIAT, and TN3K datasets. As observed, while recent SAM-adapted methods mitigate some baseline limitations, both task-specific models and existing SAM adaptations still struggle to accurately delineate boundaries in complex ultrasound images. These methods frequently exhibit blurred edges and over- or under-segmentation in challenging cases, leading to extensive false positives and negatives. In contrast, CVP-BAA consistently generates highly accurate masks with clearer boundaries and fewer segmentation errors. This superior performance could stem from the robust foundational representations of SAM, effectively leveraged and refined by our CVP and BAA modules, which explicitly inject local structural priors and enhance high-frequency boundary details. 5.1.2 Comparison on CVC-ClinicDB Quantitative Results .
